newsitem.title: BELGIUM: German gold crisis polarizes EMU options.
newsitem.headline: German gold crisis polarizes EMU options.

text.p: Germany's crisis over the Bundesbank's gold has put Europe's planned single currency at serious risk, with analysts split on whether it should be delayed or should go ahead, albeit in a broader, weaker form.

By rejecting Bonn's plan to revalue its gold reserves in a bid to bolster the government's sagging budget revenues, the Bundesbank has put in play a political dynamic that very few feel confident in gauging.
Even European financial markets have reacted cautiously, unable to assess confidently what the actual result will be.
For some analysts, however, the writing is clearly on the wall -- the odds of a delay have gone up exponentially.

They say it would be political suicide for German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to push for a single currency, one that includes a broad group of EU countries, against the desires of the German people and the central bank.
"You can't impose a new currency against the broad will of the people," said one Frankfurt-based economist. "It's political and economic suicide."

Although Kohl might get his way in the German parliament, which must now vote on the controversial measure, economists reckon the Bundestag will give the government the benefit of the doubt on one condition -- that the euro's planned 1999 start-date will be delayed.

Should the Bundestag vote against the government, the political fallout could be enormous, potentially prompting Kohl's resignation and early elections, a scenario which in itself argues against such an outcome.
"The real problem for Kohl is whether he can convince the public that a delay is worse than a broad euro," said one EU official.
Alison Cottrell, chief international economist at Paine Webber in London, put the matter more bluntly. "Under all scenarios a broad EMU has a zero percent chance," she said.

However, those who believe that EMU will go ahead on schedule, and with a large group of participants, cite one very potent argument -- that a delay would end any realistic chance of Europe ever forging a single currency.

Postponing the 1999 launch could not be credible with financial markets, which would relish the prospect of governments across the 15-nation bloc abandoning the fiscal austerity measures they have pursued for so long.
Job creation would become the issue of the day given the 18 million unemployed in the EU, and any thoughts of a delayed euro would be simply laughed at.
"In the final analysis, I think the likelihood for EMU to happen is nearly unchanged," said Ulrich Beckmann, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Franfurt.
The choice between delay and a broad euro would be unacceptable to Kohl, he added, as the chancellor is seen as a politician who in the past has mastered the fine art of negotiation.
"I think he has a good chance to get what he wants," Beckmann said. "Politics opens up many opportunities."
The one thing most analysts agree on is that Germany will finally get the kind of public debate on EMU that it desperately needs.
